record.paper_title: Euclidean random matrices: solved and open problems
record.original_question: In topologically disordered systems such as glasses and supercooled liquids, what is the origin of the Boson peak, and how important are localization properties of the vibrational modes for understanding the dynamics of supercooled liquids?

evidence.quote: In these context other interesting problems related with the high-frequency vibrational excitations of these topologically disordered systems [19] regard the origin of the Boson peak or the importance of localization properties to understand the dynamics of supercooled liquids [37].

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a topologically disordered system such as a structural glass or a supercooled liquid, modeled by atoms at off-lattice equilibrium positions interacting via a pair potential. Linearizing the equations of motion about a mechanically stable configuration yields a dynamical (Hessian) matrix whose eigenvalues $\omega^2$ and eigenvectors $\mathbf{e}_\alpha$ determine the vibrational density of states $g(\omega)$ and the spatial structure of the normal modes. The reduced density of states $g(\omega)/\omega^2$ generically exhibits a low-frequency excess above the Debye prediction, known as the Boson peak.

(a) Identify and rigorously characterize the microscopic origin of the Boson peak: determine whether the excess vibrational modes arise from (i) the disorder-induced broadening and hybridization of acoustic (sound) excitations, (ii) genuinely additional, quasilocalized soft modes associated with structural inhomogeneities, or (iii) some other mechanism, and derive the universal features of $g(\omega)$ in the Boson-peak region from first principles.

(b) Determine the localization properties of the vibrational eigenmodes across the spectrum (including the existence and frequency location of a mobility edge separating extended from localized modes, and the nature — e.g. quasilocalized vs. truly Anderson-localized — of modes in the Boson-peak region), and quantify how these localization properties affect the dynamical observables of supercooled liquids (such as the intermediate scattering function, transport coefficients, and the dynamical structure factor) above and near the glass transition.
artifact.category_tag: Euclidean random matrices and amorphous solids
artifact.status_search_result: The microscopic origin of the Boson peak and the precise role of mode localization in supercooled-liquid dynamics remain actively debated as of 2024. Recent works (Nature Physics 2022, Nature Communications 2023, J. Chem. Phys. 2023, Phys. Rev. Research 2024) propose competing or complementary pictures — quasilocalized soft modes hybridized with phonons, disorder-broadened sound waves, and structural-inhomogeneity-induced localized modes — but no single first-principles theory has been established, and the spatial structure and mobility-edge location of Boson-peak modes are still open.

status_evidence.title: Boson-peak vibrational modes in glasses feature hybridized phononic and quasilocalized excitations
status_evidence.snippet: The peak's modes are composed of many spatially coupled quasilocalized nonphononic vibrations hybridized with phonons.
status_evidence.claim: Recent (2023) work argues Boson-peak modes are hybridized phonon + quasilocalized excitations, indicating the question is still under active investigation.

status_evidence.title: The boson peak in the vibrational spectra of glasses
status_evidence.snippet: Three different scenarios have been proposed for the origin of the boson peak; none has yet fully described every aspect.
status_evidence.claim: Multiple competing theories remain, with no consensus — problem is open.

status_evidence.title: Origin of the boson peak in amorphous solids
status_evidence.snippet: Vibrations constituting the boson peak have a local character, but full spatial structure and origin remain debated.
status_evidence.claim: As of 2022 the origin remains a debated, partially understood problem.
